## Learning objectives

In this lab, we will explore historical global temperature anomalies using the NASA [GISTEMP dataset](https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/data_v4.html). We will use the `tidyverse` ecosystem to clean, summarize, and visualize climate data, and conclude by creating a simple piece of data art.

## The dataset

We will use the NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4), which provides monthly global surface temperature anomalies from 1880 to the present.

An anomaly measures the difference, in degrees Celsius, between an observed temperature and the corresponding average temperature during the reference period 1951â€“1980.

A positive anomaly indicates a warmer-than-average month; a negative anomaly indicates a cooler-than-average month.

The global CSV contains one row per year, twelve monthly columns (`Jan`â€“`Dec`), and additional seasonal and annual summaries.

Dataset: [Download NASA GISTEMP CSV](https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv)

## Importing the data

First, load the required library and import the dataset directly from NASA.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

url <- paste0(
  "https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/",
  "tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv"
)

temp_raw <- read_csv(
  url,
  skip = 1,
  na = c("***", "****"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(temp_raw)

```

The result is a wide table: each year is represented by one row, with separate columns for monthly temperature anomalies.

## Tidying the data

For many analyses, it is more convenient to have one observation per row, with separate variables for year, month, and anomaly.

```{r}
temp <- temp_raw |>
  select(Year, Jan:Dec) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = Jan:Dec,
    names_to = "month",
    values_to = "anomaly"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = month.abb),
    date = as.Date(
      paste(Year, month, "01", sep = "-"),
      format = "%Y-%b-%d"
    )
  ) |>
  drop_na(anomaly)

head(temp, n = 12)

```

## Descriptive statistics

### 4.1 Overall distribution

Let's compute basic summary statistics.

```{r}

temp |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_anomaly = mean(anomaly),
    median_anomaly = median(anomaly),
    sd_anomaly = sd(anomaly),
    min_anomaly = min(anomaly),
    max_anomaly = max(anomaly)
  )

```

These statistics describe the distribution of monthly anomalies over the entire observation period. Since the series has a strong temporal trend, the overall mean alone does not capture how temperatures have changed.

### 4.2 Comparing decades

We can investigate how the average anomaly has evolved across decades.

```{r}

decades <- temp |>
  mutate(decade = (Year %/% 10) * 10) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(
    mean_anomaly = mean(anomaly),
    sd_anomaly = sd(anomaly),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

decades

```

The most recent decade may be incomplete, so its average should be interpreted accordingly.

## 5. Statistical visualization

### 5.1 The global warming trend

We first visualize the annual mean anomaly.

```{r}

annual <- temp |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  summarise(
    mean_anomaly = mean(anomaly),
    n_months = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_months == 12) # excludes incomplete years

ggplot(annual, aes(x = Year, y = mean_anomaly)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "firebrick"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Global Temperature Anomalies",
    subtitle = "Annual means, 1880â€“present",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (Â°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

### 5.2 Comparing distributions

Next, compare the anomaly distributions across decades.

```{r}

temp |>
  mutate(decade = (Year %/% 10) * 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = factor(decade),
    y = anomaly
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature Anomalies by Decade",
    x = "Decade",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (Â°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

```

## From data visualization to data art

For the final activity, we will create a climate tapestry: a geometric composition in which each tile represents one month, and its color encodes the corresponding temperature anomaly.

### Creating the climate tapestry

```{r}
ggplot(temp, aes(x = Year, y = month, fill = anomaly)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The Fabric of Climate Change",
    subtitle = "Global monthly temperature anomalies, 1880â€“2025",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    fill = "Â°C",
    caption = "NASA GISTEMP v4 | Baseline: 1951â€“1980"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )


```


- `ggplot(temp, aes(x = Year, y = month, fill = anomaly))` maps years to the horizontal axis, months to the vertical axis, and temperature anomalies to tile colors.
- `geom_tile()` creates one rectangular tile for each month-year combination.
- `scale_fill_gradient2()` defines a diverging color palette: blue for negative anomalies, white for values near zero, and red for positive anomalies. The `midpoint = 0` argument ensures that zero corresponds to the neutral color.
- `labs()` adds a title, subtitle, legend label, and data source.
- `theme_void()` removes axes, grid lines, and other graphical elements, emphasizing the artistic composition.
- `theme()` customizes the remaining visual elements, such as the background, title size, and legend position.

The resulting artwork represents the evolution of global temperatures through color. Each tile corresponds to one month, and the gradual transition from blue to red reveals the long-term warming trend.

### Climate Spiral

Let's create a different piece of data art using the NASA GISTEMP dataset: a Climate Spiral.

Instead of representing temperatures as a rectangular tapestry, we arrange monthly observations along an expanding spiral. Each revolution represents one year, and colors encode temperature anomalies.

The resulting artwork resembles a colorful fingerprint of global warming.

```{r}
spiral <- temp |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(
    month_number = as.integer(month),
    angle = 2 * pi * (month_number - 1) / 12,
    radius = Year - min(Year) + (month_number - 1) / 12,
    ##radius = max(Year) - Year + (month_number - 1) / 12,
    x = radius * cos(angle),
    y = radius * sin(angle)
  )

ggplot(spiral, aes(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  color = anomaly
)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1.2) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The Climate Spiral",
    subtitle = expression(
      "Global temperature anomalies, 1880â€“present"
    ),
    color = "Temperature anomaly (Â°C)",
    caption = "Source: NASA GISTEMP v4"
  ) +
  theme_void()

```


- `month_number` converts the month into an integer between 1 and 12.
- `angle` determines the angular position of each month. The twelve months are distributed around a full circle.
- `radius` increases continuously over time. Each complete revolution corresponds to one year.
- `x` and `y` convert polar coordinates into Cartesian coordinates using sine and cosine.
- `geom_path()` connects observations in chronological order.
- `coord_equal()` preserves the circular geometry.
- `scale_color_gradient2()` maps negative anomalies to blue, zero to white, and positive anomalies to red.

Unlike a conventional time-series plot, the spiral visually emphasizes the cumulative passage of time. The older observations are near the center, while recent observations appear at the outer edge.

The temperature anomaly determines the color, not the distance from the center.

One caveat: this is an artistic visualization, not a precise statistical chart. The tightly packed revolutions can make individual observations difficult to distinguish. The accompanying documentation should therefore explain how the visual properties map to the data.

## Climate Flower Garden

The third and final data art visualization is something different from both the climate tapestry and the climate spiral: a Climate Flower Garden.

Each year becomes a flower with twelve petals, one for each month. The color of each petal represents the temperature anomaly, while its length also depends on the anomaly. As the years progress, the garden gradually changes from blue to red.


```{r}

library(tidyverse)

flowers <- temp |>
  filter(between(Year, 1960, 2025)) |>
  mutate(
    month_number = match(as.character(month), month.abb),
    angle = 2 * pi * (month_number - 1) / 12,
    cx = (Year - 1960) %% 10 + 1,
    cy = -((Year - 1960) %/% 10),
    # radius = 0.42,
    radius = scales::rescale(
      anomaly,
      to = c(0.18, 0.42),
      from = range(temp$anomaly, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    x = cx + 0.08 * cos(angle),
    y = cy + 0.08 * sin(angle),
    xend = cx + radius * cos(angle),
    yend = cy + radius * sin(angle)
  )

labels <- flowers |>
  distinct(Year, cx, cy)

ggplot(flowers) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = x, y = y,
      xend = xend, yend = yend,
      color = anomaly
    ),
    linewidth = 1.8,
    lineend = "round"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = cx, y = cy),
    color = "grey30",
    size = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = labels,
    aes(x = cx, y = cy - 0.52, label = Year),
    size = 2.3,
    color = "grey40"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0,
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The Climate Flower Garden",
    subtitle = expression(
      "Monthly global temperature anomalies ("*degree*C*")"
    ),
    caption = "NASA GISTEMP v4 | 1960â€“2025"
  ) +
  theme_void()

```



- `filter()` selects the years 1960â€“2025, creating a manageable garden of 66 flowers.
- `month_number` identifies each month with an integer from 1 to 12.
- `angle` places the twelve petals at equally spaced angles around a circle.
- `cx` and `cy` determine the center of each flower, arranging years in rows of ten.
- `radius` maps temperature anomalies to petal lengths using `scales::rescale()`. Higher anomalies produce longer petals.
- `x`, `y`, `xend`, and `yend` compute the Cartesian coordinates of the beginning and end of each petal.
- `geom_segment()` draws the petals, with color determined by the temperature anomaly.
- `geom_point()` adds a small dot at the center of each flower.
- `geom_text()` labels each flower with its year.
- `coord_equal()` preserves the radial geometry.
- `theme_void()` removes the usual statistical-chart elements.

The color palette uses blue for negative anomalies and red for positive anomalies. Petal lengths are scaled over the full historical dataset, making them comparable across years.

Unlike the climate tapestry, which emphasizes continuous chronological patterns, the flower garden highlights the seasonal structure of the data and allows viewers to compare individual years.

The expected visual transformation is striking: older flowers tend to contain more blue petals, while recent flowers become predominantly red.

## Final reflection

1. How does data art differ from conventional statistical visualization? 
2. Can an artistic representation communicate aspects of climate change more effectively than a traditional chart? 
3. What information might be lost in the process?
4. Do you see any bias in any of the three data artworks? How can you avoid it?

The goal of this lab is not only to analyze climate data, but also to explore how visual design can transform quantitative evidence into a compelling narrative.



## Creative challenge

Design your own piece of climate data art using the same dataset.

You are free to experiment with geometric shapes, color palettes, transparency, repetition, coordinate transformations, and visual composition.

Create an original visualization using `ggplot2` and the NASA GISTEMP dataset.

Your artwork should satisfy three requirements:

1. It must be generated programmatically from the dataset, rather than manually illustrated.
2. At least one visual property (color, size, position, shape, or opacity) must encode a numerical variable.
3. The visual composition must communicate a meaningful aspect of global warming.

You may remove conventional statistical elements such as axes, titles, legends, and labels, but you must document how the data are mapped to the artwork.

#### Representation

Each year is a ray around a circle, going clockwise from 1880. Ray length and color encode the anomaly, and the sun ends up spiky and red on the last rays.

```{r sun}
sun <- annual |>
  mutate(
    angle = 2 * pi * (Year - min(Year)) / n(),
    len = 1 + scales::rescale(mean_anomaly, to = c(0, 1.2)),
    x = cos(angle), y = sin(angle),
    xend = len * cos(angle), yend = len * sin(angle)
  )

ggplot(sun) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, color = mean_anomaly),
    linewidth = 1.1, lineend = "round"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))
```

Mapping: angle = year, ray length and color = annual mean anomaly.

#### Sunrise

Same idea as the sun, opened into a half circle: the years run left to right along the horizon, and each ray ends in a dot. The last rays rise red on the right.

```{r sunrise}
dawn <- annual |>
  mutate(
    angle = pi * (1 - (Year - min(Year)) / (n() - 1)),
    len = 1 + scales::rescale(mean_anomaly, to = c(0, 1.2)),
    x = cos(angle), y = sin(angle),
    xend = len * cos(angle), yend = len * sin(angle)
  )

ggplot(dawn) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, color = mean_anomaly),
    linewidth = 0.8, lineend = "round"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = xend, y = yend, color = mean_anomaly, size = len)
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_size(range = c(0.4, 2.2), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "#CFCFCF", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))
```

Mapping: angle = year (left = 1880, right = latest), ray length, dot size and color = annual mean anomaly.

#### Wobbling rings

Each year is a circle. Its radius grows with the year, and its outline wobbles with the twelve monthly anomalies, interpolated into a smooth closed curve. Old rings are calm and blue, recent rings are restless and red.

```{r wobbling-rings}
wobble <- temp |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  filter(n() == 12) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  reframe(
    m = seq(1, 13, length.out = 240),
    a = spline(1:13, c(anomaly, anomaly[1]), xout = m, method = "periodic")$y,
    year_mean = mean(anomaly)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    r = 2 + (Year - min(Year)) * 0.12 + 2 * a,
    theta = 2 * pi * (m - 1) / 12,
    x = r * cos(theta), y = r * sin(theta)
  )

ggplot(wobble, aes(x = x, y = y, group = Year, color = year_mean)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "#CFCFCF", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))
```

Mapping: ring radius = year, wobble amplitude = monthly anomaly, angle = month, color = annual mean anomaly.

### Delivery

Create a new folder on your GitHub repo and add:

1. an R markdown document and its rendering in HTML including the code and an explanation on how the artwork has been generated;
2. the image (PNG or JPEG) of the artwork

## Our solution

For the creative challenge we create **The ridgeline of warming**: a stack of distributions, one for each year from 1900 to today.

Each ridge shows how the twelve monthly anomalies of a year are spread. The ridges move to the right over time and the colors move from blue to red, so the warming can be seen without any axis for the trend.

### 1. Data

We reuse the `temp` table built above and we keep the years from 1900 onwards, to keep the picture readable.

```{r}
temp_ridges <- temp |>
  filter(Year >= 1900)
```

### 2. The ridgeline

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7.5, dev = "png"}
library(ggridges)

art <- ggplot(temp_ridges, aes(x = anomaly, y = as.factor(Year), fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 2.5,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    color = "#111111",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(breaks = seq(1900, 2020, by = 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "THE PLANETARY TEMPERATURE TREND",
    subtitle = "Distribution of the monthly anomalies for each year (1900-today)",
    x = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "NASA GISTEMP v4 | Baseline: 1951-1980"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(color = "gray40"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray30"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

art

ggsave("overflow.png", art, width = 10, height = 7.5, dpi = 300)
```

### What we did, step by step

1. We took the monthly anomalies from 1900 to today (each year has up to 12 values).
2. For each year we estimated the distribution of its monthly anomalies with `geom_density_ridges_gradient()`.
3. We stacked the years from the bottom (1900) to the top (today), so each ridge is one year.
4. We colored each ridge along the horizontal axis with the same blue-white-red palette used in the previous plots: the color depends on the anomaly, not on the year.
5. We removed the grid, so the shapes stand out, and we labeled one year every ten.

The ridges move steadily to the right: the monthly anomalies of 1909 are all between -0.72 and -0.32 °C (mean -0.48), the ones of 2000 are between 0.25 and 0.56 °C (mean 0.39) and the ones of 2024 between 1.16 and 1.43 °C (mean 1.28). The whole range of the data goes from -0.81 °C to 1.55 °C. A caveat: each ridge is estimated from at most 12 values, so its shape is only indicative, and the current year is incomplete.




### 3. A second artwork: the climate tree

The last artwork is a tree. Its crown is made of leaves placed one next to the other without overlapping. The horizontal position of a leaf is a year (1880 on the left, today on the right), its height is a month (January at the bottom, December at the top) and its color is the anomaly of that month: blue leaves on the left, red leaves on the right.

We build it in five steps.

#### Step 1: the positions of the leaves

We place the points on a hexagonal grid, so that every leaf has the same distance from its neighbors. The points inside an ellipse form the crown. In the corners, where the crown does not reach, we keep only 40% of the points: they are the leaves that fall or fly away, and they are needed because otherwise some months of some years (for example January 1880) would have no leaf.

```{r}
set.seed(1780)

size <- 0.06     # distance between two leaves
base <- 0.2      # bottom of the crown
height <- 1.7    # height of the crown

grid <- expand_grid(row = 0:70, col = -30:30) |>
  mutate(
    x = col * size + (row %% 2) * size / 2,
    y = base + row * size * sqrt(3) / 2,
    inside = x^2 + ((y - base - height / 2) / (height / 2))^2
  ) |>
  filter(abs(x) <= 1, y <= base + height)

leaves <- bind_rows(
  grid |> filter(inside <= 0.97) |> mutate(falling = FALSE),
  grid |> filter(inside > 1.08, runif(n()) < 0.4) |> mutate(falling = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(
    id = row_number(),
    angle = if_else(
      falling,
      runif(n(), -pi, pi),
      atan2(y - 0.65, x) + runif(n(), -0.35, 0.35)
    )
  )

nrow(leaves)
```

The leaves of the crown point away from the trunk, the falling ones point in a random direction.

#### Step 2: year, month and color

We convert the horizontal position into a year and the height into a month, and then we take the anomaly of that month from the `temp` table. The leaves with no data (the last months of the current year) are removed.

```{r}
last_year <- max(temp$Year)

leaves <- leaves |>
  mutate(
    year = round(scales::rescale(x, to = c(1880, last_year), from = c(-1, 1))),
    month = pmin(12, floor((y - base) / (height / 12)) + 1)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    temp |> mutate(month = as.integer(month)) |> select(year = Year, month, anomaly),
    by = c("year", "month")
  ) |>
  drop_na(anomaly)

head(leaves |> select(x, y, year, month, anomaly), n = 5)
```

#### Step 3: the shape of a leaf

A leaf is a pointed shape with a length slightly shorter than the distance between two leaves, so the leaves never overlap. We draw it once and we copy it on every position, rotated by its angle.

```{r}
t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 10)

outline <- tibble(
  u = c(t, rev(t)) - 0.5,
  v = c(0.4 * sin(pi * t), -0.4 * sin(pi * rev(t)))
)

leaf_polygons <- leaves |>
  cross_join(outline) |>
  mutate(
    px = x + 0.95 * size * (u * cos(angle) - v * sin(angle)),
    py = y + 0.95 * size * (u * sin(angle) + v * cos(angle))
  )
```

#### Step 4: trunk and branches

The trunk is a polygon and the branches are a few segments, thicker near the trunk and thinner at the ends.

```{r}
trunk <- tibble(
  x = c(-0.09, -0.04, -0.025, 0.025, 0.04, 0.09),
  y = c(0, 0.22, 0.58, 0.58, 0.22, 0)
)

branches <- tribble(
  ~x,    ~y,   ~xend, ~yend, ~width,
  0,     0.55,  0,     1.30,  2.5,
  0,     0.55, -0.35,  0.95,  2.5,
  0,     0.55,  0.35,  0.95,  2.5,
  0,     0.50, -0.55,  0.65,  1.8,
  0,     0.50,  0.55,  0.65,  1.8,
  0,     1.30, -0.20,  1.65,  1.1,
  0,     1.30,  0.20,  1.65,  1.1,
  -0.35, 0.95, -0.70,  1.25,  1.8,
  -0.35, 0.95, -0.45,  1.50,  1.4,
  -0.35, 0.95, -0.80,  0.90,  1.4,
  0.35,  0.95,  0.70,  1.25,  1.8,
  0.35,  0.95,  0.45,  1.50,  1.4,
  0.35,  0.95,  0.80,  0.90,  1.4,
  -0.70, 1.25, -0.95,  1.40,  0.8,
  0.70,  1.25,  0.95,  1.40,  0.8
)
```

This is the structure of the tree alone, without the leaves:

```{r, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.4, dev = "png"}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = trunk, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "#7B5338") +
  geom_segment(
    data = branches,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, linewidth = width),
    color = "#7B5338", lineend = "round"
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fff", color = NA))
```

#### Step 5: the plot

We draw trunk and branches first and the leaves on top of them, so that no leaf (that is, no data) is hidden. The leaves use the same blue-white-red palette of the previous plots. The axes are the years (bottom) and the months (left): we replace the numbers of the horizontal and vertical positions with the corresponding labels.

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, dev = "png"}
years <- c(1880, 1920, 1960, 2000, last_year)
years_x <- scales::rescale(years, to = c(-1, 1), from = c(1880, last_year))
months_y <- base + (1:12 - 0.5) * height / 12

tree_art <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = trunk, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "#7B5338") +
  geom_segment(
    data = branches,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, linewidth = width),
    color = "#7B5338", lineend = "round"
  ) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = leaf_polygons,
    aes(x = px, y = py, group = id, fill = anomaly),
    color = "grey45", linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0, guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = years_x, labels = years) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = months_y, labels = month.abb) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "THE CLIMATE TREE",
    subtitle = "Each leaf is a month: years from 1880 (left) to today (right), January at the bottom and December at the top",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fff", color = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray30"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "gray35"),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "gray40", size = 8)
  )

tree_art

ggsave("climate_tree.png", tree_art, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

| Visual property | Variable |
|---|---|
| Horizontal position of a leaf | `Year` |
| Vertical position of a leaf | month (January at the bottom, December at the top) |
| Color of a leaf | anomaly of that month and year (blue = below the baseline, red = above) |
| Trunk, branches, shape and direction of the leaves | decoration, not data |

The tree goes from blue on the left to red on the right, and the leaves in the middle, from the 1940s to the 1970s, are the palest because their anomalies are close to zero. Since the height of a leaf is its month, we can also check whether the warming depends on the season: the red on the right appears at every height. A caveat: each leaf covers about four years, because there are fewer leaves in a row than years, so a leaf shows one year of the group and not an average. The seed only fixes the small random rotation of the leaves and the choice of the falling leaves.
